responses.mission_1.search: On the open map, BFS and A* both found the same shortest path of 13.5 meters. However, BFS expanded 928 nodes, while A* expanded only 700. This means A* examined 228 fewer cells. In my code, BFS uses a queue to explore cells in the order they are discovered, without considering how close they are to the goal. A* uses the Manhattan distance heuristic along with the cost traveled so far to prioritize cells that seem closer to the goal. This helps A* explore fewer cells while still finding the same shortest path.
responses.mission_1.failure:
On the constrained map, BFS found the shortest path of 24.5 meters and expanded 848 nodes. DFS expanded fewer nodes (448), but its path was much longer at 50 meters. This is because my DFS uses a stack and explores one direction deeply instead of finding the shortest route. IDDFS reached the resource limit after 250,001 expansions because it repeatedly searches with increasing depth limits, causing it to revisit many cells.
For the unreachable case, all four algorithms (BFS, DFS, IDDFS, and A*) returned **no_path**. This means they finished searching and confirmed that no valid path existed. In contrast, **resource_limit** means the algorithm stopped because it exceeded the allowed number of expansions or time, not because the goal was impossible to reach.
I used AI to help implement and understand the algorithms. I checked the code myself by running the small tests and full evaluation, comparing the results, and checking that the algorithms returned valid paths or appropriate failure statuses.
responses.mission_2.prediction: I predict that A* will finish sooner than BFS on the constrained map. In Mission 1, both algorithms found shortest paths, but A* generally explored fewer cells because it uses the Manhattan distance heuristic to guide its search. BFS explores cells in order using a queue without considering their distance to the goal. I think A* will plan faster, although the actual navigation time may depend on the turns and obstacles along the route.
responses.mission_2.performance: I predicted that A* would finish sooner than BFS because it uses a heuristic to find a path more efficiently. On the constrained map, both planners succeeded. BFS took 89.17 seconds and traveled 23.90 meters, while A* took 89.68 seconds and traveled 23.90 meters. My prediction was not supported because BFS finished slightly faster. Both planners followed nearly identical routes, but small differences in tracking and turns can affect execution time. The plots show that even when two planners find equally short paths, the robot may not finish at exactly the same time.
responses.mission_2.choice: I would choose Nav2 as my delivery planner because it successfully reached the goal on both maps and performed consistently. On the open map, Nav2 finished in 35.50 seconds, and on the constrained map, it finished in 73.36 seconds. Compared with BFS, which took 46.40 and 89.17 seconds, Nav2 was faster on both maps and traveled shorter distances. Nav2 traveled 10.10 meters on the open map and 20.56 meters on the constrained map, while BFS traveled 13.17 and 23.90 meters. For a delivery robot, I think reliably reaching the destination while minimizing travel time and distance is more important than simply finding a path quickly.
responses.mission_3.prediction: I compared the potential field settings on both the open and constrained maps. First, I increased the repulsion strength from 0.70 to 1.30, then increased the influence distance from 1.00 m to 1.50 m, keeping the step size at 0.08 m. On the open map, both settings produced complete paths with small adjustments near the person. On the constrained map, social_1 found a complete path, but social_2 got stuck oscillating near the wall and person. This shows that stronger repulsion does not always improve navigation, especially when there is limited space.
responses.mission_3.comparison:
For A*, social_2 had the largest minimum person clearance at 0.812 m, compared to 0.733 m for the baseline. Personal-space time decreased from 1.5 seconds to 0 seconds. It also finished slightly faster, taking 46.44 seconds instead of 46.70 seconds, and traveled a little less distance (13.129 m compared to 13.192 m).
For RRT, social_1 had the largest clearance at 1.741 m, compared to 1.730 m for the baseline. Both had 0 seconds of personal-space exposure. Social_1 also finished slightly faster (43.41 seconds compared to 44.14 seconds) and traveled slightly less distance (11.522 m compared to 11.552 m).
All six trials succeeded. In these results, the wider spacing did not increase execution time or traveled distance, although the differences were small.
responses.mission_3.recommendation:
I would keep A* with social_2 for this scenario. It succeeded with a minimum person clearance of 0.812 m, took 46.44 seconds, and traveled 13.129 m. Compared to the A* baseline, which had a clearance of 0.733 m and took 46.70 seconds, social_2 kept more distance from the person without increasing travel time or distance. It also reduced personal-space exposure from 1.5 seconds to 0 seconds.
However, these trials only tested stationary people. They cannot show how the robot would react if someone suddenly crossed its path, changed direction, or stopped unexpectedly. Testing with moving people would help us understand whether the robot can adjust its route safely in real time.
responses.final.synthesis:
Throughout these three missions, I learned that a good robot route is not just about finding the shortest path. It also needs to be efficient, reliable, and safe for people sharing the same space.
In Mission 1, BFS and A* both found a shortest path of 13.5 meters on the open map. However, A* expanded only 700 nodes compared to 928 for BFS. This showed me how using a heuristic can make searching more efficient without changing the path length.
In Mission 2, I learned that faster planning does not always mean faster navigation. On the constrained map, BFS finished in 89.17 seconds, while A* took 89.68 seconds, even though both traveled 23.90 meters. Nav2 performed better overall, completing the open map in 35.50 seconds and the constrained map in 73.36 seconds. This showed how turns, obstacles, and the robot's ability to follow a path affect real execution.
Mission 3 showed why personal space matters. For A*, the social_2 setting increased minimum clearance from 0.733 m to 0.812 m and reduced personal-space exposure from 1.5 seconds to zero. However, stronger repulsion also caused oscillation in the constrained-map preview.
Overall, I think successful navigation means reaching the destination while balancing efficiency, reliability, and human comfort. The clearance, speed, and tracking values are estimates from the simulation, not perfect measurements of real-world safety. The experiments also used stationary people, so more testing would be needed to understand behavior around moving people.
responses.final.course_reflection:
This activity helped me understand how algorithms we learn in computer science are actually used in robotics. I found it interesting that two algorithms can find the same shortest path but still have different performance when the robot follows it. What stood out to me the most was the human-aware navigation part. Before this lab, I mostly thought successful navigation meant avoiding obstacles and reaching the goal. Now I understand that robots also need to consider the people around them and how their movements might affect others.
This activity made me more interested in the connection between artificial intelligence and robotics. I also realized that improving an algorithm is not always about making it faster. Sometimes making it safer and more appropriate for real-world situations is just as important.
